File `context.md`
**edulab** is a set of throwaway prototypes exploring how a user can *learn* from an agent that is doing their work for them, rather than passively watching it. See `notes/exploration.md` for the thinking and the prototype ladder, and `notes/studies.md` for the supporting literature.

Everything here is a demo, and the scaffolding constraints are deliberate. No database, no auth, no persistence, no configuration, no router. All state is client-side and in memory, discarded on refresh. The knowledge graph is likewise updated on every user interaction without asking: in any real version participation is elective and explicit (see the consent section of `notes/exploration.md`), and that is a stated constraint of the demo rather than an oversight. The backend holds no conversation state: it is a pipe from the websocket to the Anthropic SDK, and inference is streamed rather than awaited so the demo reads as a real agent session instead of a latency pause. The agentic loop is a heavily simplified take on `~/src/magenta.nvim` (anthropic only, api key only, no MCP); the web setup is lifted from `~/src/gatherus/`.

# Layout

- **`packages/iso/protocol.ts`** — the websocket message union (`ClientMessage`, `ServerFrame`). Imported by both sides.
- **`packages/backend/`** — Fastify server, entry `app.ts` (reads `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` from the root `.env`, listens on 3000). `socket.ts` registers `GET /api/socket` and is a **pipe**: it forwards the client's `MessageCreateParamsStreaming` to the SDK unexamined and streams `RawMessageStreamEvent`s back. It holds no conversation state.
- **`packages/frontend/`** — entry `main.ts`, which mounts `prototypes/chat.ts` into the page. There is one prototype and no router; later ideas land as new actions inside it rather than as separate pages. The sample picker lives in the header bar next to the layer navigation, and switching sample is a full page load.
  - `prototypes/chat.ts` — owns the thread tree, the state, and the single dispatch loop.
  - `conversation.ts` — the `MessageParam[]` plus the stream accumulator. Model, max tokens, and the system prompt are module constants here. The system prompt is deliberately **task mode**, not tutoring: learning mode is what we layer on top of the transcript it produces.
  - `view.ts` — the transcript and composer. `vamp.ts` is copied verbatim from gatherus.
- **`packages/e2e/`** — Playwright specs (`.spec.ts`, so vitest's `packages/**/*.test.ts` glob ignores them).
- **`docs/transcripts/`** — synced magenta thread archives, raw material for the prototypes. Refresh with `npm run sync:transcripts`.
- **`notes/exploration.md`** — the framing. What the learning problem actually is, why the obvious moves (student modeling, agent-as-tutor) are traps, and what we are deliberately not building. **Read this before proposing a direction or adding a prototype.** The numbered prototype sketches at the end are the roadmap.
- **`plans/`** — implementation plans, annotated with what actually happened as each stage landed.

# Commands

- `npm run dev` — vite on **5173** plus the backend on **3000**. Open http://localhost:5173. `/api/` (including the websocket) is proxied.
- `npm test` — vitest, node environment. The only unit tests are over the stream accumulator.
- `npm run test:e2e` — Playwright on its own ports (5174/3100). UI specs stub the socket with `page.routeWebSocket`, so they need no API key; `smoke.spec.ts` hits the real API and is skipped without `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`.
- `npm run sync:transcripts` — re-run `scripts/sync-transcripts.sh` to pull magenta thread archives whose `cwd` is this repo into `docs/transcripts/`. Incremental: existing threads are updated in place, so it is safe to re-run any time.
- `npm run typecheck` — `tsc --noEmit` across every package. Always run this rather than a bare `tsc`.
- `npm run lint` / `npm run lint:fix` — biome.

# Conventions

**Use the type system.** Disjoint unions over optional fields, exhaustive switches, branded ids. Prefer nominal/branded types over bare strings wherever a string is really an identifier — including map and record *keys* (`Record<ToolName, Tool>`, not `Record<string, Tool>`).

**Simplicity over abstraction.** This is prototype code with a short life. Write the concrete thing; do not build a provider abstraction or a plugin system for a second case that may never arrive. `@anthropic-ai/sdk` types are used directly rather than wrapped.

**Explicit over silent.** `RawMessageStreamEvent` is an open union we forward verbatim, so unhandled variants `console.warn` rather than throwing — but "we chose to ignore this" and "we have never heard of this" must be different branches (see `conversation.ts`).

**Single dispatch per prototype.** Each `prototypes/*.ts` owns one `dispatch` loop that calls `update` then `view.sync`. Views never hold their own dispatch. See the **[vamp skill](.magenta/skills/vamp/skill.md)** before writing any view code.

**Tests sit beside the module they assert** (`conversation.test.ts` next to `conversation.ts`), not beside the transport that reaches it. Views are verified in a real browser via Playwright, not jsdom.

**`~/src/magenta.nvim`** is a reference implementation for the agentic loop (`node/core/src/providers/`) if this outgrows itself. Do not copy from it wholesale.

File `notes/deliverable.md`
I chose option B because it struck me as the more challenging, ambiguous problem. I think I was also drawn to it because I spent so much time at Desmos thinking about how to help users learn with technology.

# ecological grounding

I started by reading up on some of the studies in this space - how are people thinking about this and measuring it currently? But I still felt disconnected from the experiences of users, so I wanted to find some transcripts of users engaging with LLMs to do work. I had an agent sample some conversations with many turns from the WildChat-1M dataset. The agent looked at random samples of messages in batches, and suggested threads for me to consider. I found that reading these was very valuable:

For example, in the "C heap file block storage" transcript, the user seems to be copy/pasting an assignment into chat and asking the agent to implement it. This user doesn't seem to be interested in engaging with their own understanding. I think things like this are really humbling, and represent the reality of how many users approach educational tools - millions of kids typing "idk" into Khanmigo. Is there anything that we can really do to get this user to engage in a learning process? What is our role in this interaction?

In the "Django event app URLs" transcript, the user is trying to build a functional prototype of an app. They seem to be genuinely interested in building and confirming that the app works, though their level of comprehension about what is happening is pretty low (they tend to just copy/paste errors to the agent).

And finally, in the "ColBERT/RAPTOR RAG design" transcript, the user is showing a lot of awareness of their own understanding and sophistication in learning strategies. This is an autodidact / power user. Hopefully we can stay out of their way, or perhaps notice ways in which our current product is interfering with their approach. For example, this user repeatedly asks the agent to summarize and restate the prompt, probably trying to keep relevant information on top of the context window.

> Let's review how chunking works... after considering both methods...

This is just from digging through ~100 chat transcripts. How incredibly useful, and what variety! If I were engaging with this as a research project, I'd probably spend way more time on just this piece. I'd try to absorb as much as I can of the texture of the problem, starting with concrete transcripts and interactions, and moving up in complexity through descriptive statistics, visualizations and more abstract ways of understanding the problem space.

But the brief was to demonstrate ability to prototype apps, so I felt like I should actually do that.

# design considerations

When embarking on the endeavor of helping people learn with technology, we must understand that such efforts have a long history of failure. I'd point to Audrey Watters' [blog](https://hackeducation.com/), and her book [Teaching Machines](https://teachingmachin.es/), or the work of education historians like [Larry Cuban](https://larrycuban.wordpress.com/). There have been many, many pronouncements about how novel technology would revolutionize education. Most did not pan out, because they started with the technology and then bent education into a shape the technology could solve.

Instead we must start with an appreciation for the incredible complexity and nuance of the teaching and learning process. Our particular technology may have very little to do with the challenge of learning. We may be offering people chat tutors, when what they actually need is a person who [cares about them](https://danmeyer.substack.com/p/five-friends-make-school-matter-to), or a work environment that treats them with dignity.

## user agency and motivation

> humans can become passive observers rather than active learners

> Ensure users grow their capabilities, not just complete tasks

The brief doesn't really speak to the user's agency. What is the user's motivation when they are engaging with the AI system? How do they relate to becoming passive observers? Are they invested in growing their capabilities?

To grow capabilities, we may choose to introduce friction into a task, like asking the user to do certain steps themselves. We may divert the user from the task in order to explore a related topic - to generalize a concept or make a connection. We may ask the user to do some additional work for us to demonstrate their understanding. If the user is coming to us with the sole goal of completing their task, these sorts of diversions will not be well received. How would the "C heap" user react if the agent responded "To ensure that you grow your capabilities, I think it's best if you implement this piece yourself"?

In order to learn, the user has to engage with unfamiliar topics and wade through confusion. Sustained, effortful attention on a learning task requires the user to provide the motivation.

So we can offer the user an invitation, but the user has to opt in.

## learning as a human endeavor

The idea of people interacting with an agent to improve their domain knowledge feels pretty depressing to me... and I think it is likely to feel demotivating to the user as well. One of the main ways we find motivation to learn is through relationships - people who care about us and our learning journey.

Outside our system, users have access to peers, mentors, coworkers, etc. We should keep an eye out for opportunities for human connection. Can our system encourage the user to engage in learning with others?

## consent, surveillance, context

A system that records everything a person does and distills it into artifacts is - in fact if not by intent - a surveillance system. There is a lot of potential for abuse. For example, such an artifact may be used by a company to algorithmically evaluate and fire employees (See Weapons of Math Destruction by Cathy O'Neil).

Interaction with such systems should be elective and explicit: the user opts in, can transparently see the information the system holds about them, and has the ability to choose how they share it, edit it, or delete it.

There is a second-order cost to getting this wrong. The fact that I am having to submit all my LLM transcripts as part of this interview definitely makes me second-guess the way I write my prompts - "does me asking this question to the LLM reflect poorly on me as an engineer?". This is distracting and undermines how I would normally engage with these tools. So we also have to be mindful of the effects of being recorded and observed on the users' behavior and attention.

And finally, we must pay attention to the broader context surrounding the human-AI interaction. A support agent using AI may be getting measured on the speed and throughput of their ticket queue. Such a person is unlikely to want to deepen their understanding. In that context, a system pushing them to grow their capabilities may just make a hostile workplace worse.

# the prototype

I ended up approaching this in two pieces.

## 1. granting the user space for reflection

Imagine you're using an LLM to complete a work task. You're reading the transcript as the agent is chugging along, and you notice something that you don't understand: perhaps a term that is unfamiliar to you or a decision that seems like it comes out of the blue.

I think the current design of many chat interfaces discourages the user from engaging with this moment. Claude's web UI will allow you to "Reply" to text from the thread, but this action inserts the message into the same thread, which interrupts and diverts the agent on this tangent. Often the explanation the agent offers leads to a second or a third thing the user may want to explore. But exploring like this also sacrifices the user's task context. An alternative is manually creating a new thread, but shuttling info back and forth between multiple threads is its own kind of friction. The user and the agent may struggle to re-orient themselves to the initial task, like the user from the RAG transcript who continually attempted to keep themselves and the agent on track via prompts like "let's summarize what we learned so far".

With this interface we are also undermining the agent's ability to attend to the task of improving the user's understanding. The system prompt and context of the main thread are oriented around completing the task, but now we're adding a secondary goal and piling it into the working context. This splits the agent's attention and prevents us from tuning the context and system prompt to the task of addressing the user's understanding.

So the first prototype attempts to ease this tension. We bring up a dedicated reflection thread, which also gives us room to experiment with the agent's context, prompt and tools.

I also notice that these sorts of reflective interactions tend to have a nested nature. In learning about a new concept, I may run into another concept that I don't understand. So the structure is a nested tree of conversations. I spent some time playing around with the UI for traversing down and back up the context stack.

This prototype reveals several opportunities for further exploration:

- how do we surface this feature to the user? I started with a top-level button to control the "reflect" layer, but found myself expecting the options to appear on text selection - a natural signal that the user wants to do something else with the text. For future directions, we could have a supervisor agent monitoring the task thread and suggest points of reflection (Confluence has a functionality where they highlight domain specific terms and abbreviations and offer a "explain this term" functionality). But I think I err on the side of not messing with the users' attention. We don't want to create a Clippy.

- what prompts do we surface to the user? I intuited "I don't understand this" and "Quiz me on my understanding" as well as a free-form question box. There could be others... like "give me some other examples of this" or "prove to me that this is correct".

- how do we help the user navigate the reflection tree? I added some UI for listing the interaction points and descending/ascending transitions (scrolling, etc.). It still feels clunky. We could add the ability to mark the reflection thread as "done" for example, or some tools for shuttling information back up to the parent thread.

## 2. Improving how the agent supports reflection activities

Within a reflection thread, the goal is attending to the user's understanding, rather than just answering the question or completing the task. This warrants a dedicated system prompt, tools and context. In particular, we want the agent to attend to the user's mental model of the domain. Can we provide the agent with some representation of the user's mental model, and would that improve the ways in which the agent interacts with the user?

One of the things I've been exploring in my coding harness work is blending LLMs with symbolic systems.

One way to do this is by creating symbolic representations and asking the agent to interact with them via tools. I explored having the agent create and maintain a [knowledge graph](https://github.com/dlants/edulab/blob/main/packages/frontend/graph.ts#L15). When using tools to interact with the graph, the agent has to model the segmentation of the domain into nodes, the modeling of the relationships between those nodes, and the segmentation of an individual concept into its description, the description of the user's understanding of the concept (and associated evidence), and a score of the user's understanding. We can also constrain how the agent can read the graph - for example by traversing nodes and edges, which forces a certain pattern of attention.

Another way to combine symbolic and neural capabilities is through automation surrounding threads. A while ago I stole this idea from Claude workflows and applied it to my own coding harness. Within this prototype, [runThread](https://github.com/dlants/edulab/blob/main/packages/frontend/thread.ts#L183) exposes an agentic thread as an async function. You provide the system prompt, tools and a yield schema; the thread runs unsupervised and yields structured data. In this case, I use this to iterate the agent's attention over each user utterance.

Opportunities for exploration exposed by this prototype are:

- does this sort of representation actually help the agent attend to the user's understanding, and produce better responses to reflection threads? (for what's "better", see evaluation below)

- can representations like this be used to enable other sorts of interactions? One sketch of this is the "Give me some ideas about what I can explore" prompt. Novices often lack the domain expertise to direct their attention productively. A condensed representation of their domain knowledge may allow the agent to help.

- how do we surface the graph to the user? I opted to show the update transcript and summary under each reflection user message, as a way of encouraging the user to look at the knowledge graph. Does seeing the graph help the user engage with their own understanding, or more effectively direct their learning?

- can the knowledge graph be useful when working with a mentor? From my experience mentoring, I think it would be interesting to see a graph like this generated from a week of my mentee's work. Perhaps it could serve as a conversation starter during a checkin? Or I could edit the graph to lay out the domain I want the mentee to learn about, or modify the descriptions to bring their attention to specific things. This would in turn affect how the agent interacted with the mentee during the week - perhaps guiding them to reflect on specific things I wanted them to look at. The notes section contains references to transcripts the mentee was performing, so perhaps during our weekly meeting I as a mentor could look at the domain graph, find nodes that I deem important that the mentee doesn't seem to have a solid grasp on, and use it as a map to jump to the more relevant transcripts to review.

I am wary of presenting this as a segmented, multi-staged approach - first we derive the graph, then we drive interventions off the graph. I think of these representations as ambiguous and malleable. Historically, knowledge graphs have been very carefully constructed by domain experts to segment the domain, since a software tutor's actions had to be deterministically driven by the graph model (I'm thinking of systems like Carnegie Learning's or Reasoning Mind's). With LLMs, we don't need to do that - here I allowed the LLMs to create the nodes based on the task context, and to loosely attach text to each node. A domain expert may look at such a representation and scoff - "these are not independent concepts, this node should be split up, etc.". However, it doesn't matter how orthogonal the knowledge graph boundaries are if the artifact positively impacts the mentee/mentor relationship, or if it helps the LLM produce better responses to the user. I am also not attached to the knowledge graph representation. Perhaps just a bucket of documents, or even a single document would work just fine. Perhaps instead of edges we just use a vector space embedding. My goal here was to demonstrate the general toolset of fusing symbolic constraints with LLMs.

# evaluation

I think the gold standard would be to have users interact with these systems at work for a prolonged period of time. We could have domain experts evaluate the users on their degree of conceptual growth during the time period. The intervention group would use the modified chat interface, the control group would use traditional AI tooling. It would be interesting to look for gradient effects with respect to overall amount of AI usage, and kind of AI usage (task completion vs reflective). This is of course rather expensive, and the outcome measure - improved domain knowledge - is one that changes very slowly and is expensive to measure accurately.

So we'd probably need to start with some process measures and see if at least we can see some signal there.

## frequency of reflective interactions

We could sample the user's messages and see how often the user is engaging in behavior that is reflective - seeking to improve their understanding, challenging the agent, asking for rationale or proof, etc. The assumption would be that if users are spending more of their time engaging in such activities then their level of domain expertise would grow. In reading some of the literature on this topic I did find this [paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.20245).

> Among participants who use AI, we find a stark divide in skill formation outcomes between high-scoring interaction patterns (65%-86% quiz score) vs low-scoring interaction patterns (24%-39% quiz score). The high scorers only asked AI conceptual questions instead of code generation or asked for explanations to accompany generated code; these usage patterns demonstrate a high level of cognitive engagement.

This study has many issues:

- small sample size
- novices learning async libraries for the first time
- a single 30min intervention
- no causal directionality (perhaps the people scored better because they're more capable, which also is why they used AI in the way that they did)

so it's weak evidence, but it's a start.

## intervention quality

We could also look at specific messages that the agent produces and evaluate them for quality. When approaching tasks like this I tend to start with quick, direct, subjective iterations and move up in scale of data and level of formality.

A lot of iteration and improvement can happen by just having the team directly working on the project spot check the transcripts. I can tell whether an agent is being useful to a junior software engineer.

Once obvious flaws stop jumping out at the reviewers, we expand to more human raters. So perhaps bringing in senior software engineers from organizations who have experience mentoring juniors. Or expanding into additional domains. Then we could have this group of people look at a larger volume of transcripts and provide feedback on interaction quality.

Once we have this corpus of human ratings, we can see if an AI model with the appropriate prompt can match inter-rater agreement with the human raters. This could expand the volume of transcripts we can rate, and allow us to set up automated improvement loops. This does carry a risk, since AI raters might have the same overall average of agreement, but exhibit a bias in its disagreement with human raters.

When we have a system that does the right thing in individual interactions, we would move to longitudinal studies of user's experiences and domain expertise growth. This is an important step since learning happens at prolonged timelines. With time, novelty wears off, people get bored or annoyed with repetition, and short term gains can wash out. I would return to direct user interviews and observations to identify low hanging fruit; then move up to more formal methods.

# scaling

## domain generalizability

This system doesn't make any assumptions about the user or the domain. However, this doesn't mean that its application to different domains will be uniform. We shouldn't test it on software engineers and then roll it out to support centers based on the engineer's data. It would be important to evaluate the system in multiple domains before assuming that improvements would generalize.

## cost / token efficiency

One major obstacle to scaling would be cost. We are creating many additional threads, and performing more iterations per user utterance. For a software engineer who's using a coding harness it's not a big leap, but for the average Claude web chat user it's a big increase in tokens spent.

The first goal in a project like this is to figure out if there is anything useful that we can do at all - using the highest-quality models, and a large amount of iteration. Once we establish a positive effect, then we can think about improving efficiency while maintaining quality.

I think there's a lot of room to make this more efficient, from using cheaper models, to gating more expensive computation behind cheaper models, to being more efficient with context through summaries or discarding things that are likely not to be relevant.

# Education Labs Take Home Assignment

## Context

As AI systems become more capable, we face two critical challenges in human-AI collaboration:

1. **Discovery & Mastery**: Users often use only a fraction of AI capabilities because they don't know what's possible or how to effectively use advanced features. This limits the value they get from AI tools.
2. **Cognitive Engagement**: When AI agents handle complex tasks autonomously, humans can become passive observers rather than active learners, missing opportunities to develop their own skills and understanding.

## Objective

Build a functional prototype that demonstrates how AI can enhance human learning and agency in one of these two areas:

### Option A: Helping users master Claude

Design a feature or system that helps users progressively discover and master AI capabilities through **integrated, contextual learning experiences** (think how video games teach complex mechanics through gameplay itself—not just tutorial videos or product tours). Your prototype should demonstrate an intuitive, creative approach to in-app learning.

Consider these angles as potential areas to address (your prototype doesn't need to solve all of these, but should thoughtfully engage with at least one):

- Help users understand what AI can do for them in context of their actual work
- Guide users from basic to advanced usage patterns through active experimentation
- Build user confidence and expertise over time via progressive challenges or achievements
- Make powerful features discoverable and learnable at the moment of need

For the purpose of this assignment, assume that the goal is to increase the complexity of workflows for users who have already been using Claude at least for a little bit, *not* onboarding beginner users to their first use cases or workflows.

### Option B: Learning through collaboration with Claude

Design a feature that helps users actively learn and develop skills while working with AI. Your prototype should demonstrate how to:

- Help users develop domain expertise (e.g., become better programmers, writers, analysts)
- Transform AI-assisted work into learning opportunities
- Build deeper understanding of subjects through AI interaction
- Ensure users grow their capabilities, not just complete tasks

## Time expectation

- <1 day (we value your time and prefer depth over breadth)

## Requirements

Create three deliverables:

1. **A functioning prototype (deployed)**
   - The Anthropic team should be able to use and interact with the prototype
   - Leverage the Claude API
   - Feel free to focus on a single feature or interaction pattern
   - Polish is less important than demonstrating your core idea effectively
2. **Your code**
   - You'll submit the code behind your functioning prototype via GitHub repo link
   - You shouldn't ignore code quality, but it's not the primary part of this activity
   - Feel free to use any languages/technologies you're comfortable with
3. **Design rationale**
   - Use both formats: self-recorded video & a short written doc outlining the problem and solution
   - Which option you chose and why
   - Your design and prototyping process to arrive at your submitted prototype
   - How your design enhances rather than replaces human agency
   - What learning principles informed your decisions
   - How you'd measure success
   - How your solution could scale to millions of users

## What we're looking for

- **Technical execution:** Can you rapidly build something functional that demonstrates your idea and iterate on it?
- **Growth-first thinking:** Does your prototype genuinely enhance learning and skill growth rather than just supporting productivity?
- **User empathy:** Do you understand the needs of learners and educators?
- **Clear communication:** Can you articulate your design decisions and rationale?
- **Creative problem-solving:** How do you approach ambiguous challenges?
- **Scalability thinking:** Can your solution generalize and work for diverse users and use cases?

## Use of Claude

You are encouraged to use Claude for both coding and any explanation artifacts. However, we are assessing your discernment and judgment in guiding Claude, not Claude's raw output. Candidates who submit Claude's outputs without demonstrating their own perspective, guidance to Claude, or design decision explanations will not pass. We want to see your thinking process - how you evaluate options, make trade-offs, and guide Claude toward executing on your ideal vision.

## Tips

- You can build features on any Claude product, not just Claude.ai!
- We highly encourage using AI tools (Claude.ai, Claude Code or your favorite AI code editor, etc.) to help you build!
- Start with a specific user journey or learning challenge rather than trying to solve everything
- Consider different user segments and how your prototype needs to fit into a product that serves multiple user segments (e.g., beginners vs power users, students vs professionals)
- 'Simple but thoughtful' beats 'complex but confusing'
- Think about how your prototype could integrate into existing AI products
- It's ok to build on top of something you've made yourself in the past, but please add to it and explain your additions

## Submission

Please submit over email:

- **GitHub repo link** with your code
- **Link to your working prototype** (can be hosted anywhere)
- **Claude transcript(s)** - Complete transcripts from Claude and / or Claude Code showing your entire interaction history with Claude for this assignment
- Your **explanation artifacts** (video + short written doc)
  - The video should involve a screenshare walkthrough of what you built
  - **Please ensure your video is no longer than 8 minutes long**

✅ You are reviewing a take-home assignment submission for Anthropic's Education La...:
**Review: Technical execution only**

Skimmed `packages/{iso,backend,frontend,e2e}`, plans/, git log.

**Strengths**
- Real, working system, not a mock. ~4.5k lines of app code + ~1.9k lines of tests, `npm run typecheck` clean across 4 packages, `npm test` green (94 tests / 10 files, <2s).
- Sharp architecture for a one-day prototype: `packages/iso/protocol.ts` (12 lines) is a tiny discriminated union; `packages/backend/socket.ts` (57 lines) is a genuinely stateless pipe that forwards `MessageCreateParamsStreaming` and streams `RawMessageStreamEvent` back. All conversation logic lives client-side. That's the correct cut for a demo and it shows judgment about what *not* to build.
- Non-trivial agent infrastructure built from scratch: `thread.ts` (713 lines) is a full streaming agentic loop with tool use, a `yield` tool with pluggable schema (`text` / `void` / custom), auto-restart nudges when the model stops without yielding (`MAX_RESTARTS = 5`), and an `answered()` check for dangling tool_use blocks. Covered by 24 unit tests. This is the piece that makes the "runThread as async function" claim in the deliverable real rather than aspirational.
- The knowledge-graph half is actually implemented and tested, not a sketch: `graph.ts` + `graph-tools.ts` (540 lines, 18 tests), `graph-view.ts` (783 lines, hand-rolled SVG with pan/zoom/arrowheads), plus citation plumbing (`citation.ts`) linking graph nodes back to transcript spans.
- Evidence of real iteration, which is the explicit criterion: ~55 commits with staged plan docs in `plans/` (7 plans, stage-by-stage commits: "Stage 1..Stage 6"), plus visible course-corrections ("Only touch the DOM when a binding's value actually changed", "Yield nothing from graph update threads", "Collapse the prototype tabs into one page"). The `task-samples/` corpus (10 real WildChat-derived threads) means the demo is seeded with real material rather than lorem ipsum.
- Test strategy is proportionate: pure logic unit-tested beside its module; UI verified in a real browser via Playwright (`chat.spec.ts` 835 lines, `graph.spec.ts` 671) with `page.routeWebSocket` stubbing so specs don't need an API key, and a separately-skippable `smoke.spec.ts` against the live API. That's a well-chosen split.

**Weaknesses / what a reviewer would ding**
- **Deployment is not done.** The brief's #1 requirement is "a functioning prototype (deployed)". There is no Dockerfile, fly.toml, render.yaml, or any deploy config in the repo. `auth.ts` (password gate over the socket) is *untracked* and the whole deploy-prep set of changes is uncommitted (11 modified, 2 untracked at HEAD `3af4d3c "Stage 3: The pane and the dispatch loop"` — mid-stage). As of this snapshot the submission would fail its hardest requirement.
- **Auth is thin.** A shared password in localStorage, checked by opening a socket and seeing if it closes, with the password in the URL query string (lands in server logs / proxy logs). Fine for a demo, but a reviewer will notice a public endpoint fronting a metered API key with no rate limiting, no per-request token cap beyond `MAX_TOKENS`, and the client choosing the model and system prompt — the backend forwards params "unexamined", so anyone with the password can run arbitrary prompts on the key. Worth one sentence of acknowledgement somewhere.
- **README is literally one line (`# edulab`).** For a GitHub-submitted take-home, no run instructions, no screenshot, no pointer to `context.md`/`notes/`. Cheapest possible fix, largest first-impression cost.
- **Two files are getting fat**: `view.ts` (1397) and `prototypes/chat.ts` (858). Defensible under the repo's stated "simplicity over abstraction" rule, and the single-dispatch convention is held, but a reviewer skimming for 10 minutes will land in `view.ts` first and see a wall.
- Stale `packages/e2e/test-results/` with an `error-context.md` from a failed graph/chat spec is committed-adjacent noise; I did not run the e2e suite (slow), so I can't confirm it's currently green — worth verifying before submitting, since a red e2e suite in a repo that advertises Playwright is worse than no Playwright.
- Opus-4.5 at 16k max tokens for every thread, including the per-utterance graph-update threads, makes the live demo slow and expensive. The deliverable's scaling section anticipates this honestly, but a reviewer clicking around a deployed instance will feel it.

**Bottom line on this criterion**: strong. The build clearly demonstrates rapid, disciplined iteration and the infrastructure (streaming tool loop, yield-schema threads, graph tools, browser tests) is well beyond what "prototype" implies for a <1 day brief. The only thing that would actually cost points is process, not engineering: ship the deploy, commit the outstanding work, write a real README.

✅ You are reviewing a take-home assignment submission for Anthropic's Education La...:
**Review: Growth-first thinking (criterion isolated)**

**Strengths**
- The core architectural move — reflection in a *separate* thread — is a real structural commitment to learning over throughput. Reflection has no path to speed up the task, so it buys only understanding. Strongest signal in the submission.
- Correctly treats motivation as something the user must opt into; explicitly refuses forced friction and the Clippy failure mode.
- The three WildChat personas (C-heap copy/paster, Django builder, RAG autodidact) do real work — design is defensible against all three, and the doc is honest that the copy/paster case isn't solved.
- Knowledge graph is framed as attending to the user's *mental model*, not task state. The mentor-checkin framing (graph as conversation starter / map into transcripts) is the most growth-first idea in the doc and points at learning-as-relationship.
- Consent/surveillance section materially constrains the learner model rather than being throat-clearing.
- Evaluation section distinguishes process vs. outcome measures and is appropriately skeptical of its own cited paper.

**Weaknesses / dings**
- **Biggest hit: the prototype demonstrates the container, not the learning.** Prototype 1 is thread routing and tree navigation (UI plumbing); prototype 2 writes a graph. Neither closes the loop where the graph changes what the agent says. The doc itself lists this as an open question, so the growth mechanism is asserted, not shown.
- Reflection is entirely user-initiated, and the doc argues the users who most need it won't initiate. Realistic beneficiary is the autodidact — the one the doc says to stay out of the way of. Unresolved tension.
- Thin applied learning-science craft: "Quiz me" is the only retrieval affordance and it's a listed prompt, not a mechanic. Spacing, desirable difficulty, self-explanation, transfer, fading support all unused. Principles arrive as ed-tech historical skepticism (Watters, Cuban) rather than as mechanisms.
- No persistence → no growth over time. Learning is defined as longitudinal, then the artifact that would carry it is scoped out. Defensible as demo constraint, but it removes the thing being evaluated.
- Graph updates every utterance without asking — self-flagged, but the demo does the thing it argues against.
- Explanation-on-demand risks being a comprehension crutch; nothing pushes toward independence.

**Net:** Above bar on growth-first *thinking* (agency, motivation, consent, limits of ed-tech — more sophisticated than most). Below bar on growth-first *demonstration* — no worked instance of a user understanding something better because of the system. Strong designer, right instincts, demo stops one step short of the criterion.

No files edited.

✅ You are reviewing a take-home assignment submission for Anthropic's Education La...:
**Review: User empathy (does the candidate understand learners and educators?)**

**Strengths**
- Transcript-reading exercise is the strongest evidence in the doc. Three concrete archetypes (assignment-dumper, prototype-builder who copy/pastes errors, autodidact) show real contact with user behavior rather than imagined personas. "Millions of kids typing idk into Khanmigo" lands because it's specific and unflattering.
- Correctly identifies motivation as the binding constraint, not interface design. The "how would the C heap user react to 'implement this yourself'" thought experiment kills a whole class of naive friction-injection designs — best empathy moment in the doc.
- Situational empathy, not just individual: the support agent measured on ticket throughput shows awareness that learning interventions land inside power structures. Most candidates never get here.
- Consent/surveillance section is genuinely user-protective; the self-observation about second-guessing his own prompts because transcripts are being submitted is a real felt datum about observation changing behavior.
- Appropriate humility about the field's failure record (Watters, Cuban) and an anti-Clippy instinct about not hijacking attention.

**Weaknesses**
- **Educators are essentially absent.** The criterion says "learners *and* educators." One speculative paragraph about a mentor reading the knowledge graph, framed as personal intuition. No educator workflow, incentives, or time constraints considered. Biggest gap.
- **Empathy stays diagnostic, never becomes design.** He establishes that the C-heap user won't opt in, then builds for the autodidact anyway. The reflection thread + knowledge graph serve the RAG-transcript power user. The two harder personas are named, sympathized with, and dropped.
- **No real users touched the prototype.** All empathy derived from dataset reading and introspection; evaluation section is entirely future tense.
- **Affect/identity underexplored.** No treatment of shame, fear of looking dumb, deadline panic, or how it feels to be *scored* on your understanding and shown that score — a notable blind spot given he wrote the surveillance section, which is the same concern one step further out.
- Some substitution of literature citation for empathy; Watters/Cuban/O'Neil establish taste, not user understanding.

**What a reviewer dings**
1. Educators ignored despite being named in the criterion.
2. Sharp user segmentation that doesn't constrain the build — insight and artifact don't meet.
3. Empathy is armchair + corpus, never contact.
4. No consideration of the emotional experience of being modeled and scored.

**Net:** above average on this criterion — transcript grounding and the motivation/context reasoning beat most submissions — but capped by the educator gap and by designing for the user he says needs the least help.

✅ You are reviewing a take-home assignment submission for Anthropic's Education La...:
Review of `notes/deliverable.md` against the brief in `docs/assignment.md`, criterion: **clear communication** only. No files edited.

## Coverage of the brief's required rationale points

- **Which option and why** — present but thin (one sentence, opening line). "More challenging, ambiguous" + Desmos is motivation, not rationale. No statement of which problem *within* Option B is being attacked.
- **Design/prototyping process** — strongest section. The WildChat transcript sampling → three user archetypes → design constraints chain is legible and is the doc's best asset.
- **Enhancing rather than replacing agency** — material exists (the "user has to opt in" argument, the consent/surveillance section) but is never explicitly tied back to the prototype. A reviewer scanning for this rubric line won't find a paragraph that answers it.
- **Learning principles** — biggest gap. Not one principle is named. "I don't understand this" / "Quiz me" are self-explanation and retrieval practice; the nested reflection tree is a cognitive-load/context-switching argument; the friction discussion is desirable difficulty. The author clearly knows this, but nothing is checkable.
- **Measuring success** — covered well. The escalation ladder (team spot-checks → expert raters → AI raters w/ inter-rater agreement → longitudinal) is crisp, and pre-empting AI-rater bias reads well.
- **Scaling to millions** — thinnest of the covered points. Only domain generalizability and token cost. Nothing on user heterogeneity (despite his own three archetypes) or what breaks at volume.

## Structural problems

- **No lede.** Brief asks for a doc "outlining the problem and solution"; there is no problem statement or solution statement up front. Reader is ~60% in (the `# the prototype` heading) before learning what was built. Needs a 3–5 sentence TL;DR.
- **Prototype under-described.** The `# the prototype` section explains *why* far better than *what*. No concrete user flow, no screenshots. A reader without the video cannot picture the interaction; the doc must stand alone since video and doc are graded separately.
- **Front-loaded skepticism.** The edtech-failure section (Watters, Cuban, Meyer) is well-argued and a credibility asset, but placed before the prototype it reads as an argument against his own submission that never resolves. Move after the build, or add an explicit "here's how I avoided that trap" landing.
- **"Opportunities for exploration" bullets overweighted.** Three long lists of open questions dilute conviction; ratio of "what I decided and why" to "what I'm unsure about" is inverted for a submission judged on articulating decisions.

## Line-level

- Long, dense paragraphs; several run 5+ connected sentences with no subheads or emphasis to anchor scanning.
- Voice is strong and distinctive — "millions of kids typing idk into Khanmigo" and the C-heap thought experiment are the most memorable lines. Keep that register.
- Defensive hedge: "But the brief was to demonstrate ability to prototype apps, so I felt like I should actually do that" — apologizes for the research detour instead of owning it.
- The Carnegie Learning / Reasoning Mind knowledge-graph paragraph is a differentiating insight buried at the end of a very long block; surface it.
- "mentee" appears with no setup in the graph section.

## Credibility risk

The cited arXiv link is `2601.20245` (dated Jan 2026) with a quoted result block. I could not verify it. If it's a hallucinated citation it will be caught, and it disproportionately damages a doc whose main strength is rigor — especially since the brief explicitly warns about submitting unvetted Claude output. **Verify before submitting.** The "this study has many issues" teardown that follows it is otherwise a highlight.

## Bottom line

Thinking is well above bar; packaging isn't doing it justice. Two fixes carry most of the value: (1) add an opening problem/solution statement plus a concrete description of what the prototype actually does; (2) name the learning principles and add a short explicit paragraph on human agency. Everything else is polish.

✅ You are reviewing a take-home assignment submission for Anthropic's Education La...:
**Review: Creative problem-solving (approach to ambiguous challenges)**

**Strengths**
- Strongest creative act is the reframe: instead of "make the agent teach," they interrogate whether the user wants to learn at all, landing on an opt-in invitation model. That's a genuine reframing of the brief, not a feature riff.
- Grounding in real WildChat transcripts before designing — the most credible signal of process. The three-user taxonomy (assignment-dumper / prototype-builder / autodidact) is their own, concrete, and does real design work.
- Core insight is specific and non-obvious: reflection is *nested*, and current chat UIs force a choice between derailing the task thread or losing context in a new one. The tree-of-threads follows directly; idea and artifact are tightly coupled.
- Names its anti-solutions (no Clippy, no supervisor agent, no deterministic student modeling) with reasons — a mark of taste under ambiguity.
- Symbolic/neural fusion (agent-maintained knowledge graph, `runThread` structured-yield) is a real technique, held loosely — they say a bucket of docs might work as well.
- Best under-developed idea: the graph as a mentor-facing map for jumping into a mentee's transcripts during a 1:1. The one place "learning as a human endeavor" becomes a mechanism rather than a caveat.

**Weaknesses / likely dings**
- More *awareness* of the design space than *resolution*. Nearly every section ends in open questions — honest on first read, hedging on second. "What did you actually decide?"
- Opt-in is asserted but the demo updates the graph on every interaction. Flagged as a deliberate constraint, which mostly holds, but the hardest problem they identified (invite without nagging) is the one the prototype doesn't attempt.
- Taxonomy is built then dropped. The prototype implicitly serves the autodidact — the user who was already going to reflect. The "C heap" user, correctly named as the humbling case, is unaddressed.
- Creativity concentrated in framing/mechanism; the surfacing layer is admittedly unresolved ("still feels clunky"). That's where the product lives or dies.
- Reflection prompts ("I don't understand this", "Quiz me") are the obvious set, self-described as intuited. Thin relative to the rest.
- Heavy front-loaded ed-tech skepticism (Watters, Cuban) is earned but risks reading as pre-emptive defense; a lot of caveat before any building.

**Net** — Top-decile on problem *finding*, mid on problem *solving*. Reads as unusually mature to anyone who's watched ed-tech fail, under-committed to anyone wanting a sharper single bet. The video needs to convert breadth into one crisp claim or the depth will be mistaken for indecision.

No files were edited.

✅ You are reviewing a take-home assignment submission for Anthropic's Education La...:
**Review — criterion: Scalability thinking**

Strengths
- Correctly separates the two axes reviewers care about: domain/user generalization and cost/token economics. Most candidates only do the latter (or neither).
- The cost analysis is honest and correctly sequenced: prove effect with expensive models first, then optimize (cheaper models, gating expensive computation behind cheap ones, context pruning). The observation that the token overhead is negligible for a coding-harness user but large for the average web chat user shows real product sense about who this can ship to.
- Refuses to assume transfer across domains ("don't test on software engineers and roll out to support centers"). Paired with the earlier point about a support agent measured on ticket throughput, this is a genuine deployment-context argument, not a hedge.
- The mentor/mentee angle in prototype section 2 is the strongest latent scaling story in the doc: the graph as a shared artifact scales the scarce resource (human mentor attention), not just the model.
- The consent/surveillance section is de facto a scaling constraint — an opt-in-only system has a very different adoption ceiling, and he names it.

Weaknesses / what a reviewer dings
- The scaling section is the thinnest in the doc (~4 short paragraphs) and reads as written last. The brief lists scalability as an explicit evaluation criterion; a reviewer skimming for it finds much less substance than for evaluation or design rationale.
- **"Millions of users" is never addressed.** No engagement with the fact that the vast majority of users are the "C heap" user who will never opt into a reflection thread. He diagnoses that user brilliantly early on, then the scaling section quietly assumes a motivated population. What is the take rate? Does the feature scale to 1M users or to the 2% who want it? This is the biggest gap.
- No serious treatment of the knowledge-graph artifact's scaling behavior over time. Does it grow unboundedly per user? How does traversal-based reading behave at 500 nodes? Does it need consolidation/decay? He says he's unattached to the representation, but doesn't say which representation scales.
- Zero engineering/infra scaling. Acknowledged prototype constraints (no DB, no auth, no persistence) are fine to leave unbuilt, but he doesn't say a word about what productionizing per-user persistent state implies. A reviewer wanting "technical execution + scalability" gets nothing here.
- No latency discussion. `runThread` iterating per user utterance is a real UX tax at scale and goes unmentioned.
- "Doesn't make assumptions about the user or the domain" is asserted, not demonstrated — every example in the doc is software engineering. The graph tools' node/edge framing may be a poor fit for writing or analysis work, which is exactly the transfer risk he warns about but doesn't probe.
- Integration-into-existing-products (a tip in the brief) is only touched glancingly via the Confluence aside. Nothing on how this lands inside Claude.ai's actual surface area or which user segments get it first.

Net: above-average scalability thinking in *quality* per sentence — the cost sequencing and domain-transfer skepticism are both correct and non-obvious — but under-weighted in volume and missing the two questions a reviewer will most want answered: opt-in rate at population scale, and how the graph behaves as it accumulates.

content.text:
All six back. Cross-cutting themes:

**Repeated by 4+ reviewers** — you diagnose three user archetypes brilliantly, then build for the autodidact, the one you said needs the least help. The C-heap user is named, sympathized with, and dropped. This is the single most-cited weakness.

**Also repeated** — the doc establishes the container (thread routing, graph writing) but never closes the loop showing the graph changing what the agent says. Growth mechanism is asserted, not demonstrated. Every section ends in open questions; ratio of decisions to uncertainties is inverted for a submission judged on articulating decisions.

**Per-criterion standouts:**
- Technical: build is strong and well beyond a one-day prototype, but *deployment doesn't exist* (no Dockerfile/fly.toml, auth untracked, 11 files uncommitted), and README is one line. Process, not engineering, is what costs points.
- Communication: no lede, no problem/solution statement, prototype under-described (a reader without the video can't picture it), and **no learning principle is ever named** despite the brief asking. Also: verify that arXiv citation `2601.20245` — a reviewer catching a hallucinated cite would disproportionately damage a doc whose strength is rigor.
- Empathy: educators are essentially absent despite being in the criterion; no treatment of how it feels to be scored and shown that score.
- Scalability: thinnest section, never addresses "millions" — take rate for an opt-in feature, and how the graph behaves as it accumulates.

Cheapest high-value fixes: ship the deploy + README, add a TL;DR with a concrete user flow, name the learning principles, and add a paragraph on what happens at population scale when opt-in is the gate.
